fail_closed_rules: Marine plans are statutory policy frameworks for marine areas; they do not by themselves grant planning permission, a marine licence, land rights or a Future Growth score.
A marine-plan policy assessment informs decision-making but is not itself the consent decision.
Section 58 marine-plan compliance must be applied to the relevant decision and cannot be converted into a generic parcel pass/fail flag.
A marine plan can apply to activities that affect a marine area even when some project elements are landward; land and sea consenting regimes must remain distinct.
Marine plan-area mapping is policy geography, not legal title, seabed ownership, harbour jurisdiction or project boundary geometry.
An inshore/offshore plan-area boundary must not be treated as a coastline, Mean High Water Springs line or cadastral boundary.
An adopted marine plan, a draft/replacement plan and historical plan-making evidence must remain temporally distinct.
The 2026 East Marine Plan replacement process does not make replacement policies adopted before formal adoption.
Marine-plan three-year reports assess relevance and implementation; they do not themselves amend every policy or grant consent.
Historical marine-plan evidence reports and iteration outputs are evidence only and must not be represented as current adopted policy.
Seascape character assessment is an evidence framework and not an automatic development prohibition or approval.
Marine-plan economic baseline statistics are area-level evidence and must not be downscaled into parcel demand, value or permission probability.
A marine licence is a separate regulatory permission and is not equivalent to terrestrial planning permission, a harbour order or landowner consent.
Planning permission does not remove the need for a marine licence where licensable marine activity is proposed.
A marine licence does not establish land ownership, seabed rights, Crown Estate consent, harbour authority consent or every other required permission.
Marine-licensing jurisdiction depends on statutory marine boundaries and tidal limits; proximity to the coast alone is not enough to infer jurisdiction.
Mean High Water Springs and Normal Tidal Limit concepts must not be approximated from ordinary coastline mapping where exact jurisdiction matters.
An exempt marine activity is not the same as an authorised unrestricted activity; exemption conditions must still be satisfied.
Eligibility for self-service marine licensing is not proof that a licence has been issued or that other consents are unnecessary.
Pre-application marine-licensing advice, screening or scoping does not equal a licence grant.
Validation or acceptance of a marine-licence application does not equal determination or approval.
Marine-licence fees and fee bands are administrative charging information, not development viability or approval evidence.
Environmental Impact Assessment screening, scoping and Environmental Statement requirements are process evidence, not the final consent outcome.
A dredging sediment sample plan or laboratory analysis does not itself authorise dredging or disposal.
An authorised dredged-material disposal site does not confer exclusive use and does not prove a specific disposal proposal will be licensed.
A marine disposal-site designation is not legal title, general planning permission or unrestricted waste-disposal capacity.
Harbour Orders are delegated legislation and must not be treated as ordinary planning permissions.
A Harbour Revision Order, Harbour Empowerment Order and Harbour Reorganisation Scheme are distinct legal instruments and must not be collapsed into one status.
A harbour-order application appearing in the public register is not proof that the order has been made.
A completed harbour-order register entry may reflect a decision or withdrawal and must not automatically be labelled approved.
A works Harbour Order can authorise specified works/powers but does not automatically establish every separate marine, environmental, land or planning consent.
Harbour jurisdiction or statutory powers do not prove ownership of every parcel or water area within a harbour.
The 2012 Ports NPS remains distinct from the July 2026 final proposed amended text until any amended NPS is formally designated.
The July 2026 proposed amended Ports NPS laid before Parliament must not be represented as already designated policy without designation evidence.
A consultation draft or proposed NPS amendment is not current adopted policy merely because scrutiny or consultation is complete.
A Ports NPS establishes national policy for relevant nationally significant infrastructure; it does not grant a DCO to an individual project.
A Development Consent Order application, acceptance or examination is not the same as a granted DCO.
A granted DCO does not by itself prove marine licence status, land acquisition completion, discharge of requirements, financing or operation.
Port freight demand forecasts are strategic evidence and not a constraint-free guarantee of future throughput at an individual port.
Port freight statistics are observed aggregated traffic and do not prove spare land, berth capacity, development rights or future commercial demand.
Provisional or scheduled port statistics releases must not be treated as published final data before their release date.
Quarterly port freight changes must not be extrapolated directly into parcel-level growth scores.
A Coastal Change Management Area is a plan designation for areas likely to be affected by physical coastal change, not a measured erosion event on every parcel.
Planning Data showing zero CCMA records is NO_DATA only and never proves that no Coastal Change Management Area exists.
Planning Data's CCMA design stage/backlog status means authoritative local-plan sources remain necessary for parcel decisions.
Shoreline Management Plans set strategic management approaches and are not planning permissions, funding guarantees or engineering designs.
Hold the Line, Managed Realignment, No Active Intervention and Advance the Line are strategic management approaches, not parcel-level consent outcomes.
An SMP management approach can change with new evidence; historical SMP documents must not override current SMP Explorer information.
Hold the Line does not guarantee that funding, construction or protection will occur for the full plan period.
No Active Intervention does not mean immediate abandonment, guaranteed erosion or automatic planning refusal.
Managed Realignment does not by itself define the final defence line, land acquisition boundary or compensation entitlement.
Advance the Line does not prove a funded or consented defence scheme exists.
SMP policy units and frontages are coastal-management geometries and are not cadastral parcels or legal ownership boundaries.
NCERM erosion-risk zones are scenario-based projections and are not predictions of an exact erosion date for a property.
NCERM scenarios with SMP delivery and no future intervention must remain separate and must not be mixed into one deterministic risk line.
Medium- and long-term NCERM extents use different horizons and climate assumptions and must not be collapsed into a single present-day boundary.
Coastal flood-defence asset datasets show assets owned, managed or inspected in the relevant system; an asset record does not guarantee a standard of protection or future maintenance.
Proximity to a flood or coastal defence does not prove a parcel is protected to a particular return period or remains developable.
Coastal authority/overview mapping is administrative reference information and not proof of land ownership, statutory responsibility for every incident or planning acceptability.
No marine/coastal source in this research-only wave may create parcel relations, Future Growth scores or business/source promotions while RECOVERY_PARKED persists.
